chapter.heading: A psalm (maskil) of Asaph.
chapter.v:
Listen to
what I have to teach you, my people; hear what I have to say.

I will
tell you wise sayings; I will explain mysteries from the past

that we
have heard before and reflected on; stories our forefathers passed down to us.

We will
not keep them from our children; we will tell the next generation about God's marvelous actions—about his power and the amazing things he has done.

He gave
his laws to the descendants of Jacob; his instructions to the people of Israel. He commanded our forefathers to teach them to their children,

so that
the next generation—children yet to be born—would understand and grow up to teach their children.

In this
way they should place their trust in God and not forget what God has done, and keep his commandments.

Then they
would not be like their forefathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation that was untrustworthy and unfaithful.

The soldiers
of Ephraim, though armed with bows, ran away on the day of battle.

They did
not keep God's agreement, and refused to follow his laws.

They ignored
what he had done, and the amazing things he had shown them—

the miracles
he had performed for their forefathers near Zoan in Egypt.

He split
the sea in two and led them through, making the water stand like walls on either side.

He led
them with a cloud by day, and by night with a light of fire.

He split
open rocks in the desert to give his people plenty to drink, water as deep as the ocean.

He made
streams flow from the stone; water rushing down like rivers!

But they
repeatedly sinned against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert.

They deliberately
provoked God by demanding the foods they longed for.

They insulted
God by saying, “Can God provide food here in the desert?

Yes, he
can strike a rock so that water gushes out like flowing rivers, but can he give us bread? Can he supply his people with meat?”

When he
heard this, the Lord became very angry, burning like fire against the descendants of Jacob, furious with the people of Israel,

for they
didn't believe in God and didn't trust him to take care of them.

Even so
he commanded the skies above and the doors of heaven to open,

and he
made manna rain down on them to eat, giving them bread from heaven.

Human beings
ate the bread of angels; he sent them more than enough food.

He sent
the east wind blowing across the sky; by his power he drove the south wind.

He rained
down meat on them as plentiful as dust; birds as numerous as sand on a beach.

He made
them fall right in the middle of their camp, all around where they were living.

They ate
until they were full. He gave them the food they longed for.

But before
they satisfied their appetite, while the meat was still in their mouths,

God became
angry with them and he killed their strongest men, striking them down in the prime of life.

Despite all
this they went right on sinning. Despite the miracles, they refused to trust him.

So he
snuffed out their futile lives, bringing them to an end in terror.

When he
began killing them, the rest came back to God in repentance, praying to him.

They remembered
that God was their rock, that God Most High was their Savior.

They flattered
him by what they told him, but they were only lying.

Deep down
they were not sincere, and did not keep the agreement they had with him.

But being
compassionate he pardoned their guilt and did not destroy all of them. He often held back his anger—he did not pour out all his fury.

He remembered
their mortality—that they were like a puff of wind that would not return.

How often
they rebelled against him in the wilderness, giving him grief in the desert!

Again and
again they provoked God, causing pain to the Holy One of Israel.

They did
not remember his strength when he rescued them from their oppressors,

performing miracles
in Egypt, doing wonderful things on the plain of Zoan.

There he
turned their rivers and their streams into blood so that no one could drink from them.

He sent
flies among them to destroy them, and frogs to ruin everything.

He gave
their crops to locusts; everything they worked hard for was taken by locusts.

He destroyed
their vines with hail, and their fig trees with freezing rain.

He handed
over their cattle to hail and their flocks to lightning bolts.

He poured
out on them his fierce anger—rage and hostility and anguish—sending a band of destroying angels against them.

He sent
his unrestrained anger against them; he did not spare them from death, handing them over to the plague.

He struck
down all the firstborn of Egypt, the first to be conceived in the tents of Ham.

But he
led out his people like sheep, and guided them like a flock in the wilderness.

He led
them to safety, and they were not afraid. He drowned their enemies in the sea.

He brought
them to the border of his holy land, to this mountainous land that he had conquered for them.

He drove
out the heathen nations before them. He divided up the land for them to own. He settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.

But they
provoked God Most High, rebelling against him. They did not follow what he had told them.

Just like
their forefathers they turned away from God and were unfaithful to him, as twisted as a defective bow.

They made
him angry with their pagan high places of worship; they made him jealous with their idols.

When God
heard their worship he became furious and he totally rejected Israel.

He abandoned
his place at Shiloh, the Tabernacle where he lived among the people.

He surrendered
the Ark of his power, allowing it to be captured; handing it over into enemy hands.

He handed
over his people to be slaughtered by the sword; he was furious with his chosen people.

Their young
men were destroyed by fire; their young women had no wedding songs.

Their priests
were killed by the sword; their widows were unable to mourn.

Then the
Lord woke up as if from sleep, as a warrior sobering up from drinking wine.

He defeated
his enemies, striking them on the back, causing them everlasting shame.

He rejected
the descendants of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.

Instead he
chose the tribe of Judah, and Mount Zion which he loves.

There he
built his sanctuary, high like the heavens, on earth that he made to last forever.

He chose
his servant David, taking him from the sheep pens,

taking him
from caring for the sheep and lambs to be a shepherd to the descendants of Jacob—God's special people, Israel.

Like a
shepherd, he took care of them with sincere devotion, leading them with skillful hands.
